title: Cost per Successful Task
body:
Overview

This record belongs to the Cost, Latency and Compute Efficiency Database (public edition), a database that measures the resources required per successful task: cost, latency, and compute, under shared accounting rules. Cost per Successful Task covers the following: divides total cost by the number of tasks that actually succeeded, not by the number attempted. The record is written as a complete, usable file: it states what the entry is, how it is used, and what its limits are, and it carries a demo program that was genuinely executed at build time, with its output stored beside the code. Benchmark honesty: this database defines part of the fixed test suite for the R32 capability collection. Its target is 99% measured reliability on defined tasks (TARGET, not measured result). The comparative measurement run comes after building and is not claimed anywhere in this round.

How it works

An efficiency measurement fixes the task list and the success definition first, then records cost, elapsed time, and compute units per task, so that resources per successful task can be compared across configurations on equal terms. Applied to this record, the method means the following in practice: divides total cost by the number of tasks that actually succeeded, not by the number attempted. The record sits at ladder rank simple in the teaching ladder, which runs simple, then compounded, then most complex, so a reader can start from the simpler records and work toward this one.

Worked example

The demo totals cost and time for a set of tasks and prints cost per successful task and mean latency. The demo program prints:

Tasks: 40, successes: 40
Cost per successful task: 3.00
Mean latency per task: 7.50 seconds

Use and limits

Efficiency figures describe the measured tasks and the measured accounting rules only. A cheaper run that fails more tasks is not more efficient once cost is counted per successful task. In practice, a reader can use this record to run the same check on their own tasks: follow the method, compare the result with the worked example, and record any difference with its evidence. The record is one of sixteen in this database, and it cross-links to related databases so the reader can continue from here without guessing where to look next.

Record details

Record fields: resource: cost; task_class: retrieval of existing records; metric: success count; sample_tasks: 100 fixed tasks.
demo_code:
tasks = 40
successes = 40
cost = 120
seconds = 300
print('Tasks: ' + str(tasks) + ', successes: ' + str(successes))
print('Cost per successful task: ' + format(cost / successes, '.2f'))
print('Mean latency per task: ' + format(seconds / tasks, '.2f') + ' seconds')
demo_output:
Tasks: 40, successes: 40
Cost per successful task: 3.00
Mean latency per task: 7.50 seconds
